name: Oil Green
lede: Oil Green is number 60 in Patrick Syme's 1821 chart of colors for naturalists, an olive gold that he pinned to a water snail's shell, an apple's skin and a beryl.

sections.title: Number 60 in Syme's chart
sections.body:
Oil Green is the sixtieth of the 110 colors in Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, filed among the greens [1][2]. It was not one of Werner's own terms [2]. Baty credits it to Johann Georg Lenz of Jena, whose mineral handbook of 1791 carried Werner's system forward under his own additions [2][3].

Syme defined it as emerald green mixed with lemon yellow, chestnut brown and yellowish grey [4]. His three examples are the common water snail with its shell, the skin of the Nonpareil apple, and a beryl [4]. That recipe sits between the cool [[emerald-green]] and the warm [[lemon-yellow]] and then dulls the mix toward brown, so the mix reads as an olive gold rather than a clean green [4].

Baty gives no reason for the word *oil*, and none of the other books we searched supplies one [2][4].

sections.title: Eggs and naturalists
sections.body:
Syme's chart was a working tool for naturalists. William Chapman Hewitson's egg book of 1833 uses number 60 for the skylark and the reed warbler [5]. Its neighbors in the same table are [[grass-green]] for the magpie, [[duck-green]] for the hooded crow and [[sap-green]] for the rook [5].

The skin of a ripe green apple is Syme's own example, so the color is easy to check against the real thing [4].

sections.title: A paint name too
sections.body:
By the nineteenth century the words were also a paint trade name. The Pigment Compendium reports Mayer (1991) treating oil green as a synonym for both Bremen green and chrome green, and it calls those two terms of variable meaning [6]. Linke and Adam list oil green among trade names in the compendium's discussion of chrome green and cinnabar green [7].

Bremen green itself appears to be a greener variant of Bremen blue [8]. Bersch listed it as a copper hydroxide, Terry linked it to green verditer, and other authors used the name for Scheele's green or emerald green [8]. So a tube labelled oil green in the 1800s need not match Syme's color, and need not share a recipe with another tube of that name [6][8].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Our library's page for Oil Green merges Syme's chart with Ridgway's plates of 1912, the ISCC-NBS names of 1955 and Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 [9]. The two Maerz and Paul entries it joins date the name differently, to about 1750 in one and to 1805 in the other [9]. The swatch is a muted olive gold, and the nearest named color in the app is [[camel]], about nine units away [9]. Syme's own chip was hand-painted and has aged, so every screen version is approximate [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,493 works, about 6.3 per cent [10]. In 75 per cent of those works it is among the lightest notes [10].

Some painters return to it far more than their peers. It appears in 14 of Luis Egidio Meléndez's 39 works here, 10 of 28 by [[painter:paulus-potter|Paulus Potter]] and 7 of 20 by [[painter:pedro-berruguete|Pedro Berruguete]] [10]. By century it peaks in the 1400s, at 8.9 per cent of paintings, and the single busiest decade is the 1710s, at 12.4 per cent [10]. Among movements, Kalighat painting from Calcutta carries it in 17 of 96 sheets [10]. Its usual company on a canvas is [[mustard]], [[khaki]] and [[olive-green]] [10].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [10]. The match says a screen color near this one was photographed, not that anyone mixed Syme's recipe [10].
